name: Marco Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, twenty-seven, and I lead the electricians on small shop refits as well as house repairs. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I like leaving a clear labelled board for whoever comes next. The tiring bit is explaining that a change requested at four o'clock won't be finished safely at five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things outside the working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ada, a library assistant, and we don't have children. I earn well, we've got nine months of expenses put away, and there are lots of other electrical firms nearby. I use AI now and then to draft plain explanations, but only after a colleague has tried the tool and I can check the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a fairly good result if the useful bits stay and the shouting settles down. I'd rather the crew got home on time than have another meeting about replacing everybody. I'd tell customers we still check the wiring ourselves, whatever writes the explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel secure carrying on. High pay and nine months saved mean I can refuse a rushed job, and there are plenty of employers around if I need a different one. I don't want a new system badly enough to be disappointed when the promises shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop-refit and repair rota now and throughout the first year. I'd continue using the explanation tool occasionally, checking every line against the completed job. I'd keep the ordinary household budget, including our weekend swimming sessions, rather than add a special AI savings target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some relief for the younger crew members. I enjoy knowing what Monday looks like, even if the work itself brings surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in an AI explanation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether it says a circuit is safe when I've only isolated it for repair. A fluent sentence can make a dangerous promise. I compare the text with my test sheet before a customer sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What lets you refuse a rushed job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings help, but so does having built a reputation for careful work. I'd still explain the time needed politely; a good wage doesn't mean I can treat customers badly.

say: I'd welcome **useful small tools** if the crew can finish work and get home on time.
I'd tell customers the **wiring checks** remain our responsibility whoever drafts the explanation.
think: My **high pay** and nine months saved make carrying on feel secure in this picture.
Nearby **electrical firms** give me options if my current employer insists on unsafe deadlines.
do: Keep the **shop-refit rota** and household budget now and through the first year.
Use the **explanation tool** occasionally, checking every line against completed work.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, enjoying familiar work without needing a dramatic change.
S0.quote: A fluent sentence can make a dangerous promise.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** follows a colleague's trial and careful checking, consistent with steady rather than early adoption.
His **existing reserve** supports turning down unsafe deadlines; keeping it unchanged is not recorded as a new saving action.

steps.text: Keep the same shop-refit and home repair rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's test one system properly before signing everybody up. Quotes and bookings might get quicker, but the apprentice still needs someone beside the board explaining each check. I'd ask our union branch to include teaching time in any deal about higher visit targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pay and practical work should hold steady for the next few years, so I'm not lying awake over it. I am uneasy about who gets trained if the office team shrinks. Someone who has spent ten years arranging our days deserves more than a link to a course after losing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd agree to a four-week paid trial of the quote tool after our estimator has tested it on finished jobs. In the first year I'd attend the union meeting about targets and ask to protect an hour of apprentice teaching each week. I'd keep the repair shifts rather than change jobs over a system we haven't even measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because the gains and the costs could land on different people. I can like a tool and still want an agreement about what changes around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you measure the quote trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compare the parts, travel and safe working time with ten finished jobs, including two that went wrong. If we use only the easy jobs, we're testing a sales pitch rather than a working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly is the teaching request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One paid hour a week when I'm not expected to take another customer call. The apprentice needs to ask an awkward question without watching my phone light up every thirty seconds.

say: I'd ask for a **proper system trial** before the whole crew is signed up.
I'd want **apprentice teaching time** protected before faster quoting becomes a higher visit target.
think: My **own practical work** and pay should hold steady over the next few years.
I worry that **office staff** might lose their jobs before useful paid training is available.
do: Run a **four-week paid trial** after the estimator tests the quote tool on finished jobs.
Attend the union meeting and seek **one paid hour** of apprentice teaching weekly.
Keep **repair shifts** while measuring what the tool really changes.
feel: **Uneasy** about the distribution of gains despite personal work and money looking safe.
S1.quote: I can like a tool and still want an agreement about what changes around it.
fieldNote: He wants **a tested tool** rather than immediate adoption, including difficult completed jobs in the comparison before expanding its use.
His **union request** is concrete: paid teaching time protected from extra customer calls, alongside concern about office staff's transition.

steps.text: Trial the quote tool for four paid weeks after estimator testing
Ask the union to protect one paid apprentice-teaching hour weekly
Keep working the repair shifts during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a licence is worth keeping, but not worth turning into a promise nobody can make. The planning work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031. I'd ask our union to negotiate paid transition work before each firm starts picking favourites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some well-paid hours as software makes quoting cheap and bigger firms chase our customers. Robots around 2031 bring another layer of pressure, and I'd only be thirty-two. Nine months saved gives me time to choose, but it doesn't make every other employer immune to the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd reserve one evening this month to compare practical equipment-servicing courses with Ada, checking workshop hours and actual paid jobs mentioned by past students. I'd enrol this year only if the course costs no more than twelve hundred and includes supervised equipment work; I can pay from a separate fifteen-hundred learning fund. In the first year after 2028 I'd seek supervised service shifts with maintained hourly pay, applying to posted vacancies if my current firm has none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can still make choices without rushing the first payment. I'd be disappointed to trade a job I do well for a course that mostly teaches me how to look busy online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you trust past students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't take one cheerful review as proof. I'd ask two people what paid tasks they actually do now and compare that with real vacancies, while remembering the jobs could change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ada's pay cover the gap if yours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only part of it, and I wouldn't assume the library role is untouched by thinking AI. Our plan starts with the nine-month reserve and a shared budget, not a promise that my partner's wage will rescue everything.

say: I'd warn that a **licence** cannot promise permanent safety from the changes described.
I'd ask the union for **paid transition work** before employers choose who gets an opportunity.
think: I could lose **well-paid hours** when cheaper planning helps larger firms chase the same repair customers.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys time, but other employers could face the same pressure when robots follow around 2031.
do: Compare **servicing courses** this month using workshop hours, past students and actual vacancies.
Enrol this year only up to **twelve hundred**, with supervised equipment work funded from the separate learning pot.
Seek **service shifts** after 2028 with maintained hourly pay, applying to posted vacancies if the firm has none.
feel: **Anxious but selective**, able to check a course before committing money.
S2.quote: Nine months saved gives me time to choose, but it doesn't make every other employer immune to the same change.
fieldNote: His **course budget** comes from a separate fifteen-hundred fund, with a twelve-hundred cap and supervised equipment work required before enrolment.
He avoids assuming **partner income** or nearby firms will remain safe, and any service shift must keep his hourly pay.

steps.text: Enrol up to twelve hundred only with supervised equipment work and checked employment evidence
Apply after 2028 for posted service vacancies with maintained hourly pay if internal shifts are unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives employers and the union time to build paid routes into different work. I'd ask for training offers to say what task and wage come afterwards, rather than promise everyone a future. A course brochure isn't a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still earn less, but five years lets me test a route without leaving a good job first. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the robots around 2034, when I'll be thirty-five. More time matters because I tend to learn best after someone else has found the first few problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose the same checked servicing course this year if it meets the cost and workshop conditions, keeping my current job while I study. In the first year after 2031 I'd request one paid supervised service day each week, only with maintained wages and the same total hours. Now I'd also join the union's training committee for its monthly meetings to help put those terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as hurried as with 2028. I can picture trying one new duty while still being useful at the work I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer offers a service day but cuts your weekly hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decline that arrangement and keep the existing rota while looking at posted alternatives. The point is to learn without quietly paying for the employer's experiment through lost wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the committee use your experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring questions from people who've already taken the course, including what equipment never worked. A useful agreement should name paid time, working equipment and somebody responsible for supervising the learner.

say: I'd ask employers and the union for **paid routes** that name the task and wage after training.
I don't think a **course brochure** should be treated as a promise of employment.
think: I could still **earn less**, but five years lets me test another route without leaving good work first.
I learn more comfortably when **other people** have found the first problems before I try a tool.
do: Take the **checked servicing course** within the same cost and supervised-workshop conditions while staying employed.
Join **monthly committee meetings** now to seek written paid-training terms.
Request **one supervised service day** weekly after 2031 only with maintained wages and total hours.
feel: **Anxious but less hurried**, imagining a gradual change alongside work he already does well.
S3.quote: A course brochure isn't a contract.
fieldNote: His **gradual route** suits steady adaptability, keeping current paid work while testing supervised service duties instead of declaring an instant career change.
The **service-day request** retains both wage and total-hours conditions, preventing reduced hours from being disguised as a training opportunity.

steps.text: Take the checked course up to twelve hundred with supervised equipment work
Request service-day training after 2031 only with maintained wages and total hours
Join monthly union training-committee meetings to seek written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to stop making every worker guess alone. I'd support public funding for paid practical learning, with employers contributing and unions checking the places are real. I'd write that to our local representative, using the course costs rather than a general complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours and income look secure over the next few years in this slower picture. Planning changes in 2036 and robots follow around 2039, when I'll be forty, so I still need a route that lasts beyond one trade label. I feel able to test things at my normal pace rather than treat every new tool as a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the checked servicing course plan now, within the same twelve-hundred cap and supervised-workshop requirement. Next month I'd write to the representative about funding fees and paid time, using the actual course timetable. In the first year after 2036 I'd join a paid trial of the new planning system only after another crew has checked it, keeping manual test records alongside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with room to enjoy the present. I'd still go swimming with Ada instead of spending every spare evening trying to guess a job title for 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you slow the course down because there is a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the course manageable beside my paid shifts, but I wouldn't postpone the first enquiry for nine years. I can learn a useful skill now without pretending I know which machines will be sold later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the representative understand about paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A free course can still cost a week's wages if it runs during working hours. Our savings let us absorb more than some people, but a public scheme should not depend on already having nine months put away.

say: I'd support **publicly funded paid learning**, with employer contributions and unions checking real places exist.
I'd write using **actual course costs** rather than ask workers to guess their future alone.
think: My **near-term hours** and income look secure while physical repair remains most of my work.
I'll be **forty in 2039**, so a longer warning still requires preparation beyond one trade label.
do: Pursue the **checked course** now within the twelve-hundred cap and supervised-workshop condition.
Write next month about **fees and paid time**, using the actual course timetable.
Trial **planning software** during paid time after 2036 only after another crew tests it, retaining manual records.
feel: **Uneasy but unhurried**, able to keep swimming and other ordinary time with his partner.
S4.quote: A free course can still cost a week's wages if it runs during working hours.
fieldNote: A **decade's warning** brings near-term security, without treating forty as an age when earned income stops mattering.
His **funding request** separates tuition from wages lost during class and does not assume others share his household's financial reserve.

steps.text: Pursue the checked course up to twelve hundred with supervised equipment work
Write next month about course fees and paid learning time
Trial planning software on paid time after crew testing, keeping manual test records

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because cheaper planning could squeeze my hours before a new route is proven. Written offers of paid supervised work would help more than telling me to be flexible. I'd also want fees and time covered for people who don't have a reserve like ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone can try a new task and come back if the training turns out badly. A trial isn't much of a trial if the old wage disappears on the first morning. I don't mind learning after someone else; I mind being told caution means I don't care.

headlineQuote: A trial isn't much of a trial if the old wage disappears on the first morning.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old crew lead** with a technical diploma and master licence, doing shop refits and home repairs.
He lives with **partner Ada**, earns higher pay, has nine months saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test tools, preferring evidence and careful trials to being first.
Quick AGI makes him **anxious about hours**; longer warnings support a capped practical course and paid duties with written wage protection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could squeeze his paid hours before a new route has been tested.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-work offers** should name supervision and preserve wages while people learn.
Training support should cover **fees and time** for people without his household reserve.
